claim: 'Why Major' and intellectual-curiosity supplements at top schools reward demonstrated intellectual engagement with a specific idea, not a resume of accomplishments in the field. Stanford explicitly frames its curiosity prompt as distinct from grades/extracurriculars; Yale asks 'why are you drawn to it'; a former Pomona associate dean names 'recapping accomplishments (already in transcripts)' as a top mistake.

application.content: For any 'why this major / what excites you intellectually' prompt: the content must be the IDEA and the writer's relationship to it, never the credential. Rule of thumb - if a sentence could be moved verbatim into the activities/awards section, it does not belong in the curiosity essay. Replace 'I founded X and won Y' with 'the question that hooked me was Z, and here is what I did with it once no one assigned it.'

Strong signal: the essay contains at least one moment of self-directed inquiry (reading, building, debating, exploring) that school did not require. Weak signal: every example of 'curiosity' is something the writer was rewarded or graded for - that reads as achievement-signaling, which is the named anti-pattern across both Stanford's framing and named-counselor guidance.

sources.citation: Application and Essays / Holistic Admission - Stanford Undergraduate Admission (intellectual vitality framed as not 'good grades or a lot of extracurriculars')

Why-Major (engagement) pairs with Why-Us (institution fit) but tests a different thing.

provenanceTrail: Verified at Tier-1 (Stanford's own framing that intellectual vitality is not grades/ECs) plus Tier-2 named former Pomona associate dean on 'recapping accomplishments' as a top mistake (on-record, dated Aug 2024). The principle is durable craft, hence semi-stable; underlying prompt wordings (cited in entries 002-003) are volatile and tracked separately.
